title: 🎙️ Repair Culture & Practical Tech
description: Today is about things you can fix, keep running, and pass on — repair culture, right-to-repair wins and setbacks, gear that outlives its manufacturer's support window, and the maker ethos of building to last rather than building to replace. We're interested in tools, devices, and projects where longevity, repairability, and self-sufficiency intersect, especially in rural and off-grid contexts where you can't just run to a repair shop. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Repair Culture & Practical Tech' — the right to repair movement, gear that outlasts its manufacturer, DIY fixes, and tools built for longevity.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical conflict; natural disasters without an engineering or preparedness angle; wildlife and conservation; working-lands policy; Indigenous governance; science discoveries with no DIY or hardware relevance; financial market news.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Hands-on hardware journalism counts fully even without an explicit right-to-repair hook.
- 80-100: Directly about repairability — right-to-repair legislation wins and losses, iFixit-style teardowns scoring repairability, gear designed for user serviceability, products outliving manufacturer support and how owners keep them running, permacomputing, vintage hardware still in active use, open-source hardware, Rossmann-style repair advocacy, 3D-printed replacement parts, battery replacement guides, rural and off-grid repair self-sufficiency.
- 55-79: Hands-on maker and DIY content — builds, modifications, hardware hacks, workshop projects, practical electronics guides with real technical depth, 3D printing hardware and filament, off-grid and solar gear, home lab hardware, tools and workshop equipment, battery and power tech. Most genuine hands-on hardware journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Gadget and device reviews with some technical substance; consumer electronics touching software longevity or ecosystem lock-in; hardware whose selling point is open firmware or modular design.
- 10-29: Surface-level product announcements, gadget speculation, leaked specs, general tech news with no hardware or repair angle.

ANCHORS: 'Framework Laptop 16 teardown: a 9/10 repairability score' → 98. 'Oregon's right-to-repair law takes effect' → 92. 'Building a solar-powered Raspberry Pi weather station' → 68. 'Samsung teases thinner bezels on next Galaxy' → 15.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A massive landslide in Alaska triggered the second-highest tsunami ever recorded, sending water and debris 1,580 feet up a mountainside just hours after tourists visited the area. Scientists discovered that the disaster was preceded by several warning signs, including rapid glacier retreat, heavy rainfall, and thousands of tiny seismic tremors. As glaciers retreat, similar disasters could become a growing danger in mountainous coastal regions.

items.title: [Nautilus] Teen Girls Are Now More Likely to Vape Than Boys
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

With the advent of e-cigarettes, millions of smokers gained a way to get their nicotine fix without many of the negative health effects of lighting tobacco on fire. Of course, because the technology is relatively new, there’s plenty we don’t know about any other adverse long-term effects. That’s one reason it’s particularly troubling that young people have adopted vaping, too. Now the latest data on youth vaping trends is out, and it’s showing some interesting gender differences. 

In a letter published today in JAMA Pediatrics, a team of researchers from the Medical University of South Carolina reports that vaping is on the rise among girls. It’s a bit puzzling. For decades, the reverse was true—more men and boys indulged in nicotine products than women. But according to data from the youth cohort for the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) study, girls have been more likely to vape than boys since 2021, with a wider gap in older teens.

Read more: “How Nicotine Disrupts the “Lung-Brain Axis”—And Could Lead to Dementia”

The post Teen Girls Are Now More Likely to Vape Than Boys appeared first on Nautilus.

items.title: [Fast Company] ‘From actually doing work’ to ‘babysitting Claudes’: Anthropic employees on how their jobs have changed in the past year
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

What’s it really like to work at Anthropic? The AI company made headlines last month when an employee resigned, claiming the company is “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” and that conversations about an AI-powered doomsday are par for the course among staff.

Now Anthropic is pulling back the curtain on its own workplace with a new report on the impact of AI adoption at the company.

Anthropic says its internal trends “could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.” If it’s right, that means a world with fewer entry-level jobs, new roadblocks to productivity, and a workforce full of babysitters for AI agents.

The babysitters club

Anthropic reports that AI is responsible for massive booms in productivity, saying its internal use of Claude tools has led to “producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.”

Its AI tools are so productive, in fact, that Anthropic now says human interference is responsible for bottlenecks in productivity. AI agents at the company spend 80% of their session time waiting for human input rather than actively working.

Though employees agree that using Claude tools improves their productivity, they say it also shifts their day-to-day responsibilities—and not always for the better.

In an April 2026 survey, 75% of Anthropic employees said they believe the company’s work processes make them productive. Responding to an open-ended question about how AI impacts their daily routines, 20% said their roles have shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes,” a task that one employee said is equivalent to babysitting children who can’t accurately gauge the importance of different tasks and problems.

“They’re like, ‘I need my juice box opened and it’s an emergency that my juice box is opened.’ And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding,” the employee said. “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

Another employee said there’s an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything,” while a third of all employees reported that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.”

When they’re not babysitting agents, the Anthropic staff’s time is also increasingly spent in meetings. The median employee spends 20% more time in meetings compared to a year ago: “A break from managing the agents typically looks like jumping into a meeting,” reads the report, adding that interviewed employees describe “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

A more senior team

As more and more work is delegated to AI agents, Anthropic’s hiring needs and practices are shifting to match. 

That means making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior hires in Anthropic’s technical departments falling from 27% to just 9% since early 2025. The overall share of junior-level technical employees also fell in the same window, shrinking from 21% to 14%.

Anthropic attributes this reduced demand for junior hires to teams offloading work to Claude, including writing code and finding bugs. AI agents at the company now work far longer hours than humans do, with interactive AI agents logging six times as many hours as human employees as of August.
